name: Max Levchin

summary.text: Max Levchin came to Chicago from the Soviet Union with his family as refugees in 1991 and earned a computer science B.S. from the University of Illinois in 1997. He co-founded SponsorNet and founded NetMeridian Software before co-founding Confinity with Peter Thiel in December 1998, then served as Confinity's and PayPal's CTO and led anti-fraud work. PayPal's 2001 S-1 shows Confinity's first money: a $100,000 bridge loan from Thiel Capital International in December 1998, later converted into Series A stock; founder shares (January 1999); a $0.5 million Series A (February 1999, about half held by Thiel Capital International); and a Series B in June and August 1999, mostly bought by Nokia Ventures, which the S-1 puts at $4.5 million in one section and $4.0 million in another. No record found of government or intelligence ties before 1999.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement

sources.publisher: Grainger College of Engineering, University of Illinois
sources.title: Max Levchin: The Making of a Tech Mogul
Max Levchin (Innovators Under 35, 2002)

facts.claim: According to the University of Illinois, Levchin and his family left the Soviet Union and settled in Chicago in 1991, entering the United States as refugees under political asylum.

sources.publisher: Grainger College of Engineering, University of Illinois
sources.title: Max Levchin: The Making of a Tech Mogul

facts.claim: Levchin received a B.S. in Computer Science from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1997.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement

facts.claim: According to PayPal's S-1, Levchin founded NetMeridian Software, 'a developer of early palm-top security applications', in January 1996 and was its CEO from January 1996 to December 1998; before that he co-founded SponsorNet, a web advertising service, where he led engineering.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement

facts.claim: The University of Illinois says Levchin's Illinois-era companies, NetMeridian Software and SponsorNet New Media, were founded with fellow students Luke Nosek and Scott Banister, and quotes Levchin saying his first company 'failed with a great bang'. No public record was found of outside investors in either company.

sources.publisher: Grainger College of Engineering, University of Illinois
sources.title: Max Levchin: The Making of a Tech Mogul

facts.claim: Forbes reported that Levchin approached Peter Thiel after a talk Thiel gave at Stanford in fall 1998 on political freedom and economic globalization, and that they started Confinity, with Thiel as CEO, in December 1998.
facts.quote: They started Confinity, an e-payments company with Thiel as CEO, in December 1998.

sources.title: Life After Facebook

facts.claim: PayPal's S-1 states Levchin co-founded Confinity Inc. in December 1998 and served as its Chief Technology Officer and a director through March 2000, when Confinity merged with X.com; he was PayPal's CTO and a director from March 2000.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement

facts.claim: In January 1999 Confinity sold 5,200,000 common shares at $0.001 per share to its executive officers; on a post-merger basis Levchin received 6,870,225 shares, Thiel 3,435,112 and Reid Hoffman 202,065.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement

facts.claim: Confinity's first preferred financing: in February 1999 it sold Series A Preferred for $0.5 million. Thiel Capital International, LLC (managed by Thiel's Thiel Capital Management) bought 2,424,785 of the 5,051,637 post-conversion shares, about half the round.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement

facts.claim: In June and August 1999 Confinity sold Series B Preferred for $4.5 million. Nokia Ventures, L.P. bought 16,165,237 of the 24,247,856 post-conversion shares (about two-thirds). Nokia Ventures partner John Malloy was a Confinity director from June 1999 to March 2000. In January-February 2000 Confinity raised $11.0 million in Series C, including Nokia Ventures and idealab!-affiliated Clearstone funds.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement

facts.claim: Forbes ASAP reported in November 1999 that Nokia Ventures and Deutsche Bank Tech Ventures were lead investors in a $4.5 million venture round Confinity closed in June 1999, and described its first product as a roughly 100 KB PayPal applet beamed between Palm handhelds by infrared to send encrypted payments.

sources.title: Capital Contagion

facts.claim: Confinity's November 1999 PayPal.com launch release named Nokia Ventures and Deutsche Bank's venture arm as investors, and listed other backers including Verifone and CyberCash founder Bill Melton, former Digicash CEO Scott Loftesness, idealab!'s Scott Banister, former HP vice president Glenn Osaka and Stanford cryptographer Martin Hellman.

sources.publisher: Confinity via PR Newswire (hosted by PayPal)
sources.title: Beaming Money by Email is Web's Next Killer App

facts.claim: Levchin and Thiel described staging a public money transfer between two PalmPilots to mark Confinity's first major funding round, which they called mainly a publicity stunt.

sources.title: Selling Investors: Beaming at Bucks

facts.claim: Levchin said PayPal's fraud losses at one point exceeded $10 million per month, describing 2000 as a year of heavy losses.
facts.quote: At one point we were losing over $10 million per month in fraud.

sources.publisher: Founders at Work (Jessica Livingston), archived copy on gwern.net
sources.title: Founders at Work: Stories of Startups' Early Days (website excerpts)

facts.claim: MIT Technology Review reported that Levchin led development of PayPal's anti-fraud program Igor, named after a Russian fraudster PayPal helped apprehend in 2000, which flags suspicious transactions so staff can freeze accounts; it said the FBI had also enlisted Igor against wire fraud. It named him 2002 Innovator of the Year.
facts.quote: The FBI has also enlisted Igor to combat wire fraud.

sources.title: Max Levchin (Innovators Under 35, 2002)

facts.claim: InfoWorld reported that, to build Igor, Levchin first let internet fraudsters steal money so he could observe their methods and design countermeasures. It called the strategy risky because it involved the possible loss of money. The report describes a study tactic, not cooperation with fraudsters.

sources.title: Max Levchin, PayPal

facts.claim: In the S-1 (as of September 2001) Levchin beneficially owned 5,152,668 PayPal shares (2.6%). The University of Illinois later put his stake at about 2.3%, worth roughly $34 million, when eBay acquired PayPal for $1.5 billion in 2002.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement

sources.publisher: Grainger College of Engineering, University of Illinois
sources.title: Max Levchin: The Making of a Tech Mogul

facts.claim: Levchin and engineer David Gausebeck built a sign-up test, later called the Gausebeck-Levchin test, to stop programs from opening PayPal accounts automatically. In a 2023 Sequoia podcast, which places it in PayPal's summer-2000 fraud crisis, Levchin said real-time account creation then fell by about 50%. Eric Jackson's 2004 book says it made automated opening of accounts linked to stolen credit cards effectively impossible.

sources.title: PayPal: A Merger of Enemies That Reshaped Silicon Valley

sources.publisher: World Ahead Publishing (Eric M. Jackson; text via Internet Archive full-text search)
sources.title: The PayPal Wars: Battles with eBay, the Media, the Mafia, and the Rest of Planet Earth

facts.claim: Levchin said in 2023 that a fraudster who was creating fraudulent PayPal accounts found his email address. He said he received about half a dozen emails a week from the person, somewhere in Eastern Europe, critiquing his anti-fraud measures, until the sign-up test took effect.
facts.quote: half a dozen of emails per week from this person somewhere in Eastern Europe

sources.title: PayPal: A Merger of Enemies That Reshaped Silicon Valley

facts.claim: In a January 21, 2004 Stanford talk with Peter Thiel, Levchin said PayPal was losing about $12 million a month to fraud in June 2000, on top of costs such as referral bonuses. He said fraud had been well above 1% of volume at its peak; the transcript gives the end-2001 rate as both about 0.55% and about 0.37%, and about 0.49% in mid-2001. The transcript does not label speakers; this opening section is attributed to Levchin because the speaker refers to 'Peter and I'.

sources.title: Coping with Fraud — Max Levchin and Peter Thiel

facts.claim: Newsweek reported in July 2001, quoting CTO Levchin, that PayPal's anti-fraud team built software named 'Igor' after a Russian mobster who had plagued the system the previous year. It said prosecutors in the Ivanov/Gorshkov case would get help from computer logs and testimony from PayPal's anti-fraud team, and that PayPal executives said they had helped bust organized-crime rings in Chicago, Houston and Nigeria.

sources.title: Busting the Web Bandits

facts.claim: MIT Technology Review reported in December 2001 that Levchin's Igor system combined rules and a neural network, with people reviewing the evidence before freezing accounts. It said Igor at one point became overzealous and prompted employees to deactivate many legitimate users, followed by complaints to the Better Business Bureau. It also described PayPal verifying bank accounts by making two tiny deposits for users to confirm.

sources.title: Digital Cash Payoff

facts.claim: American Banker reported in 2006 that Levchin called the Igor software 'basically, the reason we survived'. The paper said Igor's namesake was a con artist PayPal never caught; according to PayPal, he gave up and moved on to easier prey.

sources.title: How a Scam Artist Helped the Art of Monitoring

connections.claim: Levchin co-founded Confinity with Peter Thiel in December 1998; Thiel was CEO and Levchin CTO. Thiel's S-1 biography says he had been managing member of Thiel Capital Management since 1996 and previously traded derivatives for CS Financial Products.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement

connections.claim: Levchin founded SponsorNet New Media and NetMeridian Software at the University of Illinois with fellow students Luke Nosek and Scott Banister; Nosek later joined him in the Bay Area at Confinity.

sources.publisher: Grainger College of Engineering, University of Illinois
sources.title: Max Levchin: The Making of a Tech Mogul

connections.claim: Levchin's Illinois companies were founded with Scott Banister; by November 1999 Banister, then a vice president at idealab!, was listed as a Confinity backer.

sources.publisher: Grainger College of Engineering, University of Illinois
sources.title: Max Levchin: The Making of a Tech Mogul

sources.publisher: Confinity via PR Newswire (hosted by PayPal)
sources.title: Beaming Money by Email is Web's Next Killer App

connections.claim: Levchin was Chief Technology Officer and a director of Confinity (December 1998 to March 2000) and of PayPal from March 2000; PayPal's S-1 named him and Thiel as the key executives whose loss could harm the business.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement

connections.claim: Nokia Ventures, L.P. bought most of Confinity's $4.5 million Series B in mid-1999, and its partner John Malloy joined Confinity's board in June 1999, serving alongside Levchin as a director until the March 2000 merger.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement

connections.claim: MIT Technology Review reported in 2002 that the FBI had enlisted Igor, the PayPal anti-fraud program Levchin led, to combat wire fraud. No public record was found of any government or intelligence tie to Levchin before 1999.

sources.title: Max Levchin (Innovators Under 35, 2002)

connections.claim: As PayPal CTO, Levchin led the response to scripted mass sign-ups in 2000, including the Gausebeck-Levchin test. No record was found of him being accused of any part in bonus abuse.

sources.title: PayPal: A Merger of Enemies That Reshaped Silicon Valley

openQuestions: Accounts of the 1998 Levchin-Thiel meeting differ: Forbes (2011) gives the talk's subject as political freedom and economic globalization; secondary sources say currency markets and that a former co-founder (possibly Nosek) told Levchin about it. The Forbes 2018 interview (Stephanie Denning) and Levchin's Stanford eCorner transcript could not be opened.
Forbes (2011) says Levchin 'had sold his previous company' before meeting Thiel, while the S-1 says he ran NetMeridian until December 1998. No record found of a sale, buyer or price.
No record found of who, if anyone, funded SponsorNet or NetMeridian (1995-1998).

Reported amounts from Thiel at the founding breakfast ($200,000-$300,000) come only from secondary sites; the S-1 shows only the January 1999 founder share purchase and Thiel Capital International's Series A stake.
The size of Deutsche Bank Tech Ventures' stake in the 1999 Series B is not disclosed in the S-1 (it was below the 5% reporting level by 2001).
The identity of the Russian fraudster Igor was named after, and the 2000 apprehension PayPal helped with, were not verified from a court or DOJ record in this session.
Secondary accounts disagree on the 1999 'beaming' demo amount ($3 million vs $4.5 million) and on its date.
Founders at Work (2007) records Levchin saying 'Bob and I built this package called IGOR'; the co-builder's full name was not confirmed in this session.
